results.description:
I followed Tone Fuentes’ video on creating a Portra 400 style lightroom preset a while ago and have been pleased with the results. This is my attempt to port that over to an OM-3 recipe. It’s warm, lifts the mid tones a little and seems to work well with a lot of shots (versatile, like the film). This is my attempt to approximate that preset in terms of OM-3 settings.

The second version dials down the Amber white balance adjustments for a more subdued warmth.
An attempt to emulate the X-T30 Velvia recipe on the E-M10 mark 2.

I like the look of vintage film stocks. This recipe combines fluorescent WB with a slight magenta shift, while the curve lifts the shadows and brings down the mids and highlights. The 12 colors are kept at a lower intensity to give the images a more subdued, vintage feel.
I created this mono recipe by referencing scans from my own Ilford HP5 rolls.
Slightly less contrast than Acros, with just small nudges from OM's default MONO 1 profile — a touch more midtone punch, highlights pulled back a hair, and a bit of warmth in the white balance.

This profile was produced by a color matching script shared by ibd on camaraderie forums. Acros was known for its fine grain and sharp details. These settings are a light touch on the baseline with slight drop in shadows, slight raising of mid tones, slight bump in contrast.

Kodachrome 64 Printed On Ilfochrome
Profile created from Kodachrome 64 and Ilfochrome paper specifications.
Printing technique simulates "Silver Mask" trick with Yellow and Magenta filter pack
Leans heavily into teal & orange. Fun for night street photography
Estill Springs Green - warm and feels like fall y'all

Tokyo-Wetzlar Profile is a digital CCD sensor emulation defined by its mid tone-driven tonal density and warm-neutral color bias -- qualities drawn from the Kodak CCD sensor heritage shared by Olympus cameras engineered in Tokyo and Leica cameras developed in Wetzlar.
It distinguishes itself through selective color emphasis, restrained contrast, and a rendered quality that favors depth over clinical accuracy. Its visual signature is characterized by luminous, amber-leaning reds, deep and saturated blues, and deliberately suppressed greens producing images that feel weighted, painterly, and quietly cinematic without exaggeration.
Kodak CCD sensors were developed as a digital equivalent to 'Film'. Kodaks vast knowledge of color science and chemistry was the base.
Enhances saturation for complementary colors along the orange/blue axis, slightly raises shadows and mids and drops shadows. Adds a minor blue/magenta shift to white balance.

Not a simulation of any single film stock, but a synthesis of classic monochrome principles translated through the OM-3 system. 
The X-Monochrome profile produces images with:

• Strong mid-tone presence
• Controlled, luminous highlights
• Anchored shadows with depth
• Smooth tonal transitions
• Natural separation without harshness
• A subtle, print-like cohesion

It is particularly well suited for architecture, street photography, and portraiture—situations where light defines structure and where tonal relationships matter more than color contrast.
Note the white balance shift to Blue. The Base White Balance configuration applies a deliberate blue-weighted luminance bias prior to
monochrome conversion.This is a critical adjustment. While black-and-white imagery contains no color information in its final form, digital sensors generate luminance through the weighted interaction of red, green, and blue channels. Adjusting white balance at this stage directly influences how the TruePicX processor constructs the values before the image is rendered as monochrome.

Lots of contrast, sharpness, and a strong red filter evoke the ethos of Ansel Adams and other classic black and white landscape photographers. The red filter darkens blue skies and further increases contrast.

With this recipe I tried to emphasise the colours I see in my local rural environment, without overdoing the blue skies, while also managing the harsh Australian light. I prefer warm tones so there’s a lot of amber in the white balance shift. I’ve currently set the Keep Warm Colour to off, but after testing it turned on I’m now undecided. The name was suggested by a member of the OM3 Recipes Facebook group (thank you for that inspiration).
This recipe emphasizes the saturation of cool tones, raises mids, and increases sharpness. It's intended for shooting the vibrant colors of early spring.

The OM-3 Fujicolor 200 Film Emulation Profile, is a refined consumer color negative emulation defined by its balanced, daylight-true palette and subtle cool bias—qualities that made it a reliable staple for everyday photography across a wider range of conditions. It distinguishes itself through clear color separation, moderate contrast, and a naturalistic rendering that favors clarity over overt warmth. Its visual signature is characterized by yellow-leaning greens, gently cyan-shifted blues, and warm but controlled reds, producing images that feel crisp, grounded, and quietly vibrant without exaggeration.

The Night Mayor is a tribute to the city after dark — to quiet streets, artificial light, and moments that often go unnoticed.
Named in honor of Rotterdam and its iconic Night Mayor, Jules Deelder, it reflects a way of seeing the city: calm, raw, and alive at night.

Built for night photography, but tested across mixed light, interiors and even daylight, it maintains contrast, color separation and atmosphere without falling apart.

I set the ISO range at a standard of 800 with a maximum range of 6400.

Note: This recipe is tuned for a tungsten white balance and was created with a 1/4 gold mist filter. If you’re not using a similar filter, your results may differ — adjust as needed to match your taste.
A recipe dedicated to the Pacific Northwest. I emphasizes cooler colors, reduces contrast and sharpness to evoke the misty, hazy, overcast feeling to capture the spirit of the region.
My daily go-to recipe
A cinematic color profile inspired by the carefully constructed world of Asteroid City, where everyday locations are transformed into quiet, stylized scenes.

CityEurope is a recipe designed for the hobbyist photographer who wants a single color profile that works equally well in urban environments and natural landscapes.
The color dial pushes saturation heavily into the cyan, teal, and green range — giving skies that distinctive blue-green shift reminiscent of European analog films from the 1970s and 80s. Warm tones are kept restrained: reds and magentas sit at zero, letting the cooler palette dominate without making skin tones look unnatural.
Highlights are pulled down aggressively (-5) to tame the harsh contrast between sun and shadow that photographers face on city streets and open landscapes. A gentle midtone lift and raised shadows keep the image from going too dark, preserving detail in the lower register.
The result is a cool, film-inspired look with rich skies and a subtle vintage character — ready straight out of camera.

This recipe is inspired by the RAW output of the Leica Q. Files from the Leica Q itself were used, along with information from the ‘Leica Q116 Preset (DF)_2020’ from Red Dot Forum. In my opinion, Olympus produces some of the most pleasing RAW files among current camera brands. For this reason, when compared to this recipe, you may notice a slight increase in color saturation, as well as more pronounced adjustments to shadows and highlights, along with added contrast. On very sunny days, you may lower the midtones to -1 or -2 if desired.
Des couleurs très saturées, le bleu de la mer est profond et vibrant, un vert chaud et intense, un contraste marqué, un rendu plutôt "punchy presque carte postal !
Based on the DXO Film Pack 5 preset.

Kodachrome 64 is an iconic color film celebrated for its vibrant, rich color saturation and exceptional sharpness, underpinned by an extremely fine grain structure. It masterfully combines rich depth with a subtle color reproduction that results in striking images. The film is particularly known for delivering punchy reds and distinct blue skies, creating a saturation level that enhances scenes with a poetic quality. This unique palette taps deeply into "memory color" and nostalgia, solidifying its legendary status in photography.

This formula targets the signature look of Kodak Portra 400, a professional color-negative film celebrated for its natural color, gentle tonality, and exceptional rendering of people. The heart of this emulation is Portra’s ability to hold both highlights and shadows with grace, producing images that feel open, smooth, and forgiving rather than contrasty or harsh. This is achieved in-camera by slightly lifting the shadows, gently compressing highlights, and shaping the midtones to create Portra’s characteristic soft, luminous tonal flow. The result is a subtle, film-like "creamy" look that preserves detail across the scene without appearing flat. Color is tuned to prioritize skin tones, maintaining Portra’s hallmark neutral-warm balance with a delicate, flattering warmth that keeps faces natural and lifelike, making this profile especially well suited for portraits, travel, and editorial-style photography.

Kodak Gold 200 is a quintessential consumer color negative film, defined by its warm, emotionally resonant palette and forgiving exposure latitude—qualities that established it as a cornerstone of everyday photography from the late 20th century through the early digital transition. It distinguishes itself not through bold saturation, but through approachable vibrancy, gentle contrast, and a perceptual warmth that feels inherently human. Its visual signature is characterized by magenta-leaning reds, restrained greens, and softly cyan-inflected shadows, producing images that feel simultaneously nostalgic and alive.

For added warmth, use in-camera raw editor, add a Yellow/Orange hue color creator effect with level +2.

Fujicolor SUPERIA Premium 400 is a quintessential consumer color negative film, celebrated for its warm, emotionally resonant color palette and forgiving exposure latitude, making it a staple of everyday photography throughout the late 20th and early digital transition era. It is distinguished not by dramatic saturation, but by its ability to render scenes with approachable vibrancy, soft contrast, and a perceptual warmth that feels inherently human. SUPERIA's visual signature is built around magenta-leaning reds, restrained greens, and gently cyan-inflected shadows—producing images that feel simultaneously nostalgic and alive.

Kodachrome 64 is an iconic color film celebrated for its vibrant, rich color saturation and exceptional sharpness, underpinned by an extremely fine grain structure. It masterfully combines rich depth with a subtle color reproduction that results in striking images. The film is particularly known for delivering punchy reds and distinct blue skies, creating a saturation level that enhances scenes with a poetic quality. This unique palette taps deeply into "memory color" and nostalgia, solidifying its legendary status in photography.

This variant has slightly less amber and slightly deeper shadows.

Dirty Pop: Named after a popular NSYNC song, this is a natural but punchy color with deep shadows and a gentle highlight lift. Greens and yellows get a little glow, blues run a touch darker, which keeps skies rich and skin tones clean straight out of camera.

This color profile is my “Red Soda Pop”. It warms up the overall tones, makes the reds "pop" while muting yellows and greens ever so slightly. It also softens the image for a bit more dream-like feel.

This look delivers rich contrast with cooler tones, featuring softer greens and a versatile neutral balance that works across almost any subject.

Vibe: Clean, neutral, contrasty but calm. Think Fuji Provia or 400H.
Best for: Sunset, travel, versatile light
Avoid in: Flat or overcast light. It can look a little lifeless.

Nostalgic Summer is a vintage inspired recipe that focuses on vibrant greens and golden yellows while stripping away blues for a more timeless look. Ideal for capturing contrasty, sunny days by delivering a filmic look straight out of camera.

Dave Herring shared these settings to dial in a vibrant chrome profile emphasizing reds. It’s based on the COLOR 3 default, but drops saturation of greens and uses a custom white balance of 5200K for daylight with B+1, M+1 adjustments.

For this edit, I built a look that feels true to my style desaturated blues, warm mids, and those orange-red tones that really pop. It’s all balanced with a subtle filmy curve that gives it that nostalgic, cinematic finish for the golden hour.
A desaturated look that leans into reds and oranges, inspired by Amy Shore's photography.

This is where I captured the wild beauty of exotic plants and brought their colors to life through my lens, amplifying the saturated greens of the lush jungle canopy and intensifying the vivid magentas and warm tones of tropical blooms to recreate the untamed vibrancy of the rainforest.

This color profile boosts warm and cool tones while dialing back greens and magentas, letting complementary colors stand out. With softer contrast, lifted shadows, lowered highlights, and reduced sharpness, the result feels balanced, natural, and true to the scene.

This recipe comes from Ali for One Month Two Cameras. She describes it as golden, punchy, a bit of kodak warmth. She recommends using it for cooler, mid-day, dappled light. Suggests avoiding indoors or golden hour. Vibe: Golden, punchy, rich skin tones. A bit of that Kodak warmth.
Best for: Cool early morning or midday sun, beachy or dappled light, clean outdoor scenes
Avoid in: Indoor tungsten or golden-hour light. It gets too warm.

Vibe: Meyerowitz/Cape Light. Soft, dreamy, pastel with luminous highlights.
Best for: Overcast, open shade, late afternoon or blue hour
Avoid in: Harsh sunlight. It washes out fast.

💡 Slightly overexpose for a softer feel.

Vibe: Slide film feel. High punch, crisp edges, moody shadows.
Best for: City scenes, golden hour, strong shapes
Avoid in: Overcast or extreme contrast without careful metering

💡 Slightly underexpose and use your histogram. This one can clip highlights fast.
OM-CHROME was designed to capture the vibrant colors of daily urban life geared to emulate the classic look of 35mm positive slide film.

results.recipeName: Emily's Custom Color Profile With Custom White Balance
results.description: This gives a more stylized look with a warm feel. Works well outdoors.

This is the Slim Aarons inspired Kodachrome 64 simulation that James Bloomer shared in this post. This version lowers the contrast and scales back some of the saturation. The instructions say to under expose, so I’ve included that in the EV compensation.
This profile was designed by Gareth B.. It’s like KODACHROME 25, but crushes shadows more and knocks back yellows and purple even more.

This profile was shared by Gareth B. in a mu-43.com post. Shadows are crushed, highlights and midtones merged. Yellows, blues, and greens are knocked back. Orange and red are enhanced. Gareth notes that heavily desaturated greens were a characteristic of Kodachrome 25. 
Source: mu-43 post via Rob Trek’s YouTube video. Note: In Rob’s video and Gareth’s post WB should be -2 Amber and +2 Green. Also see Henry Richardson’s post in dpreview forums.

This profile was generated by ibd’s script to match images created with a fuji camera’s Velvia film simulation. It’s interesting to compare it to other velvia approximations. It’s also interested to consider it alongside qualitative descriptions of the film. This old article from fujifilm-x.com provides some interesting notes — like enhancing magentas to make the blues more memorable.

The profile for provia ended up very close to the default COLOR1 setting. The only differences are a small shift toward Amber and Green, and a small bump of green saturation. This seems to match the description on the fujifilm site describing a provia simulation as an even balance in both saturation and tonality dimensions, making it versatile and robust for a variety of situations. This is very similar to what Olympus/OM System choose as their default.

Fuji Pro Neg Standard (or Pro Neg. Std) is a portrait-oriented film simulation characterized by soft, muted tones and a gentle, understated color palette. It renders skin tones with particular delicacy-- warm but not oversaturated, with a slightly cool, creamy quality that flatters complexions. Shadows are lifted and open rather than deep and crushed, giving the image a low-contrast, airy feel. Colors across the board are desaturated. Greens are subdued and earthy, blues are soft and quiet, and highlights retain detail with a gentle rolloff rather than blowing out abruptly.

Fuji Pro Neg Hi (Pro Neg. H) shares the same portrait-oriented DNA as Pro Neg Standard but with a notably higher contrast and slightly more saturated rendering. Skin tones remain flattering and natural,  but they carry a bit more warmth and richness — a touch more depth in the reds and oranges without tipping into the exaggerated. Shadows are deeper and more defined than Pro Neg Std, giving images a greater sense of dimensionality and presence, while highlights still roll off smoothly without harsh clipping. Colors have more punch overall — greens feel slightly more alive, blues a bit more assertive  — but the simulation never crosses into the vivid territory of Velvia; it remains fundamentally a film stock about rendering reality with polish rather than drama. The increased contrast makes it more versatile than Pro Neg Std across a wider range of lighting conditions, performing well not just in controlled studio settings but also in open shade or overcast outdoor light where the added depth helps prevent images from feeling flat or lifeless.

Fuji Eterna Cinema is a motion picture negative stock defined by deliberate restraint — colors are desaturated and neutral across the board, with no single hue asserting itself, and skin tones carry a slightly cool, gray-green cast rather than warmth. Shadows are famously lifted and milky, resisting crushed blacks and holding detail throughout the dark end of the tonal range, while highlights roll off gradually without clipping. Overall contrast is intentionally low, producing a wide dynamic range negative designed to give colorists maximum post-production latitude rather than delivering an opinionated look in-camera. The cumulative effect is understated and cinematic — a cool, expansive, emotionally neutral canvas built to be shaped rather than admired straight out of the gate.

The om-3 Classic Neg recipe by ibd produces a warm but tonally complex look built around a significant amber white balance shift (+4) tempered by a green push (+3), giving the image a warm-but-not-golden overall cast with a subtle vintage green undertone. Reds and orange-reds are nudged up while yellows and greens are pulled back, which shapes skin tones to feel rich and saturated without going overly orange — closer to the slightly faded warmth of classic negative film stock. The most distinctive color move is the strong boost to blue and cyan (+4 each) paired with a hard cut to cyan-green (-5), which carves out a cool, filmic separation in skies, shadows, and any blue or teal elements — giving those areas real pop against the warm mids. Tonally, the recipe has a lifted, airy quality: mids are raised considerably (+6) and highlights are opened up (+3), while shadows are ever so slightly compressed (-2), all combined with a -0.7 EV exposure pull that keeps the overall image from feeling too bright. The result is a recipe that feels simultaneously warm and cool depending on where you look — organic and analog in the midtones and skin, with crisp, slightly cinematic blues — well-suited to street and travel photography in varied natural light.

results.description: This slightly desaturates almost every color, drops exposure slightly, raises mids to compensate, and adds another point of amber.  CLASSIC CHROME is the color analog to monochrome film. Tonality (contrast) is the key. It’s the opposite of Velvia — taking color out and focusing on the tonality or contrast to make the picture. In fujifilm’s description the shadows are hard, but towards the highlights contrast gets softer. I think this is what pushing the mids accomplishes.

Jack Wang tweaked Isaac’s classic chrome recipe (blog, youtube). It looks like the main tweak was increasing contrast by bumping highlights and dropping shadows more dramatically. In my one sample image, I do find the result slightly more pleasing than the original classic chrome.

Astia is a portrait film. It should be close to ProNeg Hi, but with more saturation and more tonality. It’s designed for natural light and action shots. It shouldn’t wash out in highs. The softness is reportedly limited to skin tones, and shadows are hard to add sharpness.

It shifts the colors and softens things up. Combines high saturation and low contrast. 

I think this recipe SHINES in urban environments. It’s also amazing in the garden (although it’s worth experimenting - not all colors work here.)
Adjusting color for unique looks has a history going back to the invention of color film. I love how these create a soft, dreamy, glowing look.
Manual describes it as “a light and soft color tone.” It mimics soft chrome film. This drops yellows way down to -4, and drops purple/blue back -1. Highlights +3, shadows -3.

Manual describes it as “a film-like effect with high saturation and rich colors. Similar to Kodak Ektrachrome according to Isaac Mitropoulos in his excellent OM-3 review post. This basically takes the vibrance up to +4 for everything except purple, which only gets +3. Similarly highlights are boosted +4 and shadows dropped -4. Basically this is cranking colors and contrast up to maximum.

Described in the manual as “a color tone with depth and richness. Similar to Kodachrome 64 according to Isaac Mitropoulos in his excellent OM-3 review post. Yellows and blues are slightly enhanced (+1) while reds and greens slightly more subdued (0). Highlights are boosted +3 and shadows dropped -3.
Described in the manual as “the standard natural preset.” All settings are at 0. This provides the baseline that customizations can be built on.

City Look is a color-only recipe with a completely neutral tone curve — no shadow lifting, no highlight adjustments, no exposure comp — letting the color channel work do all the heavy lifting. The dominant moves are a strong boost to yellows (+3) and a hard cut to cyan (-5), which together push the image toward a warm, electric, urban palette reminiscent of sodium street lighting and city glow while stripping out the cool teal tones that would otherwise balance it. Orange-reds are significantly pulled back (-4), which prevents skin tones and warm surfaces from going ruddy or oversaturated, keeping warmth in the yellow register rather than the orange-red one — a more artificial, neon-adjacent quality than natural warmth. The result is a recipe that feels distinctly metropolitan: punchy and warm in the yellows, stripped of cool-teal neutrality, with enough restraint in the reds to keep it from feeling like a simple warming filter.
